summary.text: Let \(p=16843\), whose primality follows by excluding divisors through \(\sqrt p=129\); a finite modular evaluation of \(H_{p-1}\) shows \(H_{p-1}=p^3R\) with the denominator of \(R\) coprime to \(p\). Splitting \(H_{p^2-1}\) into terms whose indices are divisible by \(p\) and the remaining terms, then pairing each remaining index \(x\) with \(p^2-x\), yields \(H_{p^2-2}-1=p^2S\) with denominator coprime to \(p\), so \(p^2\) divides the reduced numerator minus denominator although \(p^2\) is composite.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
H_m=\sum_{k=1}^m\frac1k
\]
be the \(m\)-th harmonic number, and write it in lowest terms as
\[
H_m=\frac{N_m}{D_m},\qquad D_m>0,
\]
with \(\gcd(N_m,D_m)=1\). Thus the sequence in question is
\[
a(m)=N_m-D_m.
\]
(The formal definition uses the absolute value of this difference, but for every \(m\ge 2\), \(H_m>1\), so \(N_m>D_m\) and the two descriptions agree.)

We will exhibit the composite integer
\[
n=16843^2=283686649
\]
for which
\[
n\mid a(n-2).
\]
This directly contradicts the asserted equivalence between this divisibility and primality.

Set
\[
p=16843,
\qquad M=p^2=283686649.
\]
We first record two finite arithmetic facts about \(p\).

First, \(p\) is prime. Indeed,
\[
129^2=16641<16843<16900=130^2,
\]
and direct trial division gives a nonzero remainder upon division of \(16843\) by every integer \(d\) with \(2\le d\le129\). Therefore \(16843\) has no divisor between \(2\) and its square root, and hence is prime. In particular \(p\ge3\) and \(p\) is odd.

Second, we need a particular congruence for \(H_{p-1}=H_{16842}\). We describe the finite computation that establishes it.

For positive integers \(L\) and nonnegative integers \(d\), define an integer pair \((U_{L,d},V_{L,d})\) recursively. At depth zero put
\[
(U_{L,0},V_{L,0})=
\begin{cases}
(1,L),&L<p,\\
(0,1),&L\ge p.
\end{cases}
\]
At the next depth, combine the two adjacent blocks by the usual addition-of-fractions rule:
\[
\begin{aligned}
U_{L,d+1}
 &=U_{L,d}V_{L+2^d,d}+U_{L+2^d,d}V_{L,d},\\
V_{L,d+1}
 &=V_{L,d}V_{L+2^d,d}.
\end{aligned}
\]
An induction on \(d\) gives
\[
\frac{U_{L,d}}{V_{L,d}}
 =\sum_{\substack{L\le i<L+2^d\\ i<p}}\frac1i.
\]
Indeed, at depth zero this is immediate, and the induction step simply splits the interval of length \(2^{d+1}\) into its two consecutive subintervals of length \(2^d\) and adds their fractions. All the \(V_{L,d}\) are positive.

The same recursion can be performed modulo any chosen modulus: at each leaf reduce the pair modulo the modulus, and after every addition and multiplication reduce again. Induction on the depth shows that the resulting pair is exactly
\[
(U_{L,d}\bmod m,\;V_{L,d}\bmod m).
\]
For \(L=1\) and \(d=15\), the interval has length \(2^{15}=32768\), while the cutoff \(i<p\) retains exactly \(i=1,2,\ldots,16842\). Thus
\[
\frac{U_{1,15}}{V_{1,15}}=H_{16842}=H_{p-1}.
\]
The finite modular recurrence described above gives
\[
(U_{1,15},V_{1,15})\equiv(0,169067457020)\pmod{p^3},
\]
where
\[
p^3=4778134229107,
\]
and, separately,
\[
(U_{1,15},V_{1,15})\equiv(0,16842)\pmod p.
\]
Only the first coordinate of the first congruence and the second coordinate of the second congruence are needed. They say
\[
p^3\mid U_{1,15}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
p\nmid V_{1,15},
\]
because \(16842\equiv-1\pmod p\).

Write \(U_{1,15}=p^3K\), with \(K\in\mathbb Z\), and define
\[
R=\frac{K}{V_{1,15}}.
\]
Then
\[
H_{p-1}=p^3R.
\]
Moreover, when \(R\) is reduced to lowest terms, its denominator divides \(V_{1,15}\). Since \(p\nmid V_{1,15}\), we have
\[
p\nmid\operatorname{den}(R).
\tag{1}
\]

We next analyze \(H_{p^2-1}\). Partition the integers \(1,2,\ldots,p^2-1\) according to whether or not they are divisible by \(p\). The multiples of \(p\) in this interval are precisely
\[
p,2p,\ldots,(p-1)p.
\]
Their reciprocal sum is
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{p-1}\frac1{pj}
 =\frac1pH_{p-1}
 =\frac1p\,p^3R
 =p^2R.
\tag{2}
\]

It remains to treat the terms whose indices are not divisible by \(p\). Let
\[
\mathcal T=\{x:1\le x<p^2,\ p\nmid x\}.
\]
The map
\[
x\longmapsto p^2-x
\]
is a fixed-point-free involution of \(\mathcal T\). It maps the lower half of the interval bijectively onto the upper half. To see that it preserves \(\mathcal T\), note that if \(p\mid p^2-x\), then, since \(p\mid p^2\), subtraction would give \(p\mid x\), contrary to the definition of \(\mathcal T\). It has no fixed point because \(p^2\) is odd, so \(p^2/2\) is not an integer.

Choose one representative from each pair, namely those satisfying
\[
1\le x<\frac{p^2+1}{2},\qquad p\nmid x,
\]
and define
\[
T=\sum_{\substack{1\le x<(p^2+1)/2\\p\nmid x}}
\frac1{x(p^2-x)}.
\]
For every such representative,
\[
\frac1x+\frac1{p^2-x}
 =\frac{p^2}{x(p^2-x)}.
\]
Summing this identity over the representatives gives
\[
\sum_{x\in\mathcal T}\frac1x=p^2T.
\tag{3}
\]
Combining (2) and (3), we obtain
\[
H_{p^2-1}=p^2R+p^2T=p^2(R+T).
\tag{4}
\]

We will need careful control of denominators. We use the elementary fact that if a prime \(p\) divides none of the denominators of finitely many rational numbers in lowest terms, then it does not divide the denominator of their sum in lowest terms. For two fractions, the reduced denominator of their sum divides the product of their denominators. Thus, if \(p\) divided the reduced denominator of the sum, primality of \(p\) would force it to divide one of the original denominators. The assertion for any finite sum follows by induction. The same observation applies to differences.

For every summand of \(T\), neither \(x\) nor \(p^2-x\) is divisible by \(p\). We already know \(p\nmid x\), and if \(p\mid p^2-x\), then again \(p\mid x\). Hence
\[
p\nmid x(p^2-x).
\]
The denominator in lowest terms of \(1/[x(p^2-x)]\) is exactly \(x(p^2-x)\), so the preceding finite-sum observation gives
\[
p\nmid\operatorname{den}(T).
\tag{5}
\]

Now put
\[
q=H_{p^2-2}.
\]
Since the next harmonic term is \(1/(p^2-1)\), equation (4) yields
\[
q=H_{p^2-1}-\frac1{p^2-1}
  =p^2(R+T)-\frac1{p^2-1}.
\]
Subtracting \(1\), and using
\[
1+\frac1{p^2-1}=\frac{p^2}{p^2-1},
\]
we find
\[
\begin{aligned}
q-1
 &=p^2(R+T)-\frac1{p^2-1}-1\\
 &=p^2(R+T)-\frac{p^2}{p^2-1}\\
 &=p^2\left(R+T-\frac1{p^2-1}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
Define
\[
Y=R+T-\frac1{p^2-1}.
\]
Then
\[
q-1=p^2Y.
\tag{6}
\]

We claim that the reduced denominator of \(Y\) is not divisible by \(p\). By (1), the reduced denominator of \(R\) is not divisible by \(p\), and by (5) the same is true for \(T\). The denominator of \(1/(p^2-1)\) is \(p^2-1\), which is congruent to \(-1\pmod p\), so it too is not divisible by \(p\). Applying the denominator observation first to \(R+T\) and then to its difference with \(1/(p^2-1)\), we conclude that
\[
p\nmid\operatorname{den}(Y).
\tag{7}
\]

It remains to translate (6) into the desired statement about the numerator minus denominator of \(q\). Write both rational numbers in lowest terms:
\[
q=\frac ND,
\qquad
Y=\frac AB,

after choosing \(D,B>0\). Equation (6) becomes
\[
\frac ND-1=p^2\frac AB,
\]
or equivalently
\[
\frac{N-D}{D}=\frac{p^2A}{B}.
\]
Cross-multiplication gives the integer identity
\[
B(N-D)=p^2AD.
\tag{8}
\]
By (7), \(p\nmid B\), and therefore \(\gcd(p^2,B)=1\). Equation (8) shows that \(p^2\mid B(N-D)\). Euclid's lemma, using \(\gcd(p^2,B)=1\), now gives
\[
p^2\mid N-D.
\tag{9}
\]

Here \(q=H_{p^2-2}\), so \(N-D=a(p^2-2)\). Also \(p^2-2\ge2\), hence this difference is positive; even under the absolute-value convention, (9) gives exactly
\[
p^2\mid a(p^2-2).
\]
Thus, with
\[
n=p^2=16843^2=283686649,
\]
we have \(n>2\) and
\[
n\mid a(n-2).
\]
However, \(n\) is not prime: it is the square of the integer \(16843>1\). Therefore this \(n\) satisfies the divisibility condition but fails the primality condition. Consequently the conjecture
\[
\text{for every }n>2,\quad n\mid a(n-2)\iff n\text{ is prime}
\]
is false.
